extracted.intended_audience: readers of 19th-century literature; students and scholars of fiction and social commentary
extracted.subtask_description: Extraction of evaluative principles and didactic statements embedded in a late-19th-century novel chapter (characterisation, pedagogy, preaching, language). The page is a narrative excerpt that contains several implicit criteria about teaching, religion, language, and moral conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: True teacher's role
rubrics_metrics.description: The true teacher is the one who is able to guide those instincts, strengthen them with authority, and illuminate them with revelation of their own fundamental truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best instruction sometimes consists in not interfering with a pupil's natural instincts; the teacher should guide and strengthen innate tendencies with authoritative direction and illuminate them by revealing their fundamental truth. Anti-pattern: imposing external methods that suppress the pupil's instincts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivate learning through practical interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical interest is the strongest incitement to a theoretical acquaintance (e.g., Alec's interest in building a boat led him to translate Virgil about ships).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Connect theoretical material to learners' concrete pursuits or projects; real practical engagement can produce genuine theoretical understanding. Example: a boy learning classical lines about rigging because he wanted to rig a boat. Anti-pattern: expecting abstract study to motivate learners without linking to their interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconciliation as moral victory
rubrics_metrics.description: To make a friend of an adversary is the only victory that can give true satisfaction—reconciliation is morally superior to triumph by domination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where conflict exists, seek reconciliation and friendship rather than asserting authority or winning a contest; the emotional and moral gains of reconciliation outweigh victories obtained by subjugation. Example: the master resolving antagonism with Alec by kindness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective religious teaching must vivify, not merely moralise
rubrics_metrics.description: The parish (muckle kirk) often delivers 'the dry banes of morality' without the living wind of the Word, whereas mission preaching can be 'rousin'' and life-giving.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Religious instruction (and by extension any moral teaching) should impart life and inward conviction, not only abstract moral precepts; practical rousing preaching can be more effective than dry moralising. Anti-pattern: dull, purely moral lectures that fail to stir conviction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity of belief in a leader matters more than rhetorical splendour
rubrics_metrics.description: A minister's authentic personal belief and the real relation of his heart to God give him a reverent authority in the eyes of listeners, even if some doctrinal views are flawed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess religious (or moral) leaders by the sincerity and inward reality of their conviction rather than solely by doctrinal precision or intellectual display. Example: Annie's reverence for Mr Brown persists because she senses his real faith.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique of authoritarian pedagogy
rubrics_metrics.description: An autocratic schoolmaster whose pleasure is law and who rewards submission (and punishes deviation) exemplifies a cruel, hypocritical model of instruction (e.g., whipping orphans while later feeding them liquorice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid teaching models that prioritize obedience to rules over learners' welfare and moral development; corporal punishment and favoritism are condemned here as signs of bad pedagogy and hypocrisy. Example/anti-pattern: daily whipping of helpless children justified by a parent invoking 'spare the rod'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language/dialect should be judged by literary vitality, not dismissed as 'patois'
rubrics_metrics.description: Scotch (Scots) is not merely a patois; it has a living literature and directness and simplicity that are virtues even if later polished forms acquired other advantages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate dialects by their expressive resources and literary tradition rather than dismissing them as inferior; value directness and simplicity in speech. Anti-pattern: treating vernacular speech as inherently inferior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conception of 'song' versus 'epic' as a criterion of poetic form
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'song' is perceived to 'turn round' and come to an end, whereas an epic (as the child perceives of Paradise Lost) 'goes on and on' without the cyclical closure of a song.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When selecting poetry or assessing suitability for a listener (especially children), prefer shorter ballad-forms that close and return over sprawling epics that the listener may not experience as 'song'. Example: Annie prefers ballads because they have the recurrent, ending structure of songs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral/emotional effects of preaching can induce terror or consolation
rubrics_metrics.description: Sermons emphasizing God's wrath and eternal torments can produce overwhelming terror and despair in sensitive listeners, while small consolations (a kindly hand, lozenges) may mitigate immediate distress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the psychological impact of moral or religious rhetoric on vulnerable audiences; choose tempering pastoral care and empathy when discussing severe doctrines. Anti-pattern: delivering terrifying depictions of punishment without pastoral consolation.
